title.en: Alberto and the Monsters: Seven Heads, Ten Heads, Twelve Heads
title.zh: 阿爾貝托降魔記：七首、十首、十二首

region.en: Casiguran (Tayabas coast) and Sinucuan (Mt. Arayat) — Philippine frame for an imported tale, Luzon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋卡西古蘭與蘇努庫安（外來故事之在地框架，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters', eBook #8299

summary.en: A whirlwind carries off King Luis's three daughters; Prince Alberto of Sinucuan wins the magic boot, rusty key, and invisibility hat from quarrelers, drinks the monsters' pails of water until his iron chairs and beds break under him, and cuts off the seven-, ten-, and twelve-headed monsters head by head through the invisible door. Restoring all three princesses before the third day, he picks his bride by the handkerchief he slipped to the youngest.
summary.zh: 旋風捲走國王路易的三位女兒；蘇努庫安王子阿爾貝托以巧計贏得魔靴、鏽鑰與隱身帽，飲下魔怪的水桶直至鐵椅鐵床應聲而碎，隔著隱身之門將七首、十首、十二首巨魔逐一斬首。三日之限前送回三位公主，並以悄悄塞給幼女的手帕擇定新娘。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler connects it to the Servian storm-stolen princesses (Wuk No. 5), the Bear's-Son underworld monsters, and Strong Hans (Grimm No. 166); Sinucuan is the legendary King of Pampanga of Mt. Arayat, who figures in the corpus record pampangan-crow-black-sinukuan.

passages.text: Once there was a king in Casiguran named Luis, who had three beautiful daughters, the youngest the fairest of all. One day the three princesses went to the orchard to amuse themselves; it happened that on that day the wind blew very hard, and they were swept away. The king felt very sad over the loss of his daughters, and issued proclamations in all parts of his kingdom, saying that anyone who could find his daughters within three days would be allowed to choose one of the three for his wife. At that time there was also in the neighboring kingdom of Sinucuan a king who had a brave son named Alberto; when Alberto heard of the matter, he went to the king and said that he would look for his lost daughters, and King Luis accepted his offer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Prince Alberto walked and walked until he came to a large forest where he found two boys fighting over a boot which, if worn by anyone, would carry him to whatever place he wanted to go, provided he kicked the ground. 'Go over by that large tree, and the one who can run here first shall have the boot,' said the prince — and while the boys were walking toward the tree, he put on the boot and kicked the ground, and was at once carried far away. In the same manner he won from two young men a rusty key which, knocked against a stone, would open the stone however hard it might be, and from two old men a hat which made its wearer's body invisible. The boot brought him before a huge rock with a small hole in it; Alberto put the key in the hole, and the rock suddenly opened, revealing a street leading to a palace, where a beautiful princess met him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before Alberto could say a word, the princess told him to go away, for a seven-headed monster was living with her; 'If that is the case, show me his sword, and I will kill him.' The sword was too heavy for him to move — until the princess gave him a pail of water to drink, the water the monster always drank before touching his sword; he drank it and sat down on an iron chair, and the chair broke. 'The princess now told him that he was strong.' Soon steps were heard on the stairs: Prince Alberto put on his hat and stood by the door, sword in hand. When the monster came up, he thrust one of his heads through a window near the door and said, 'I smell something human!' — and the prince cut off that head. 'Somebody must be here!' cried the monster, but the princess answered that there was no one there with her; the prince then cut off the monster's heads one after another until only the main one was left, and when at last the monster entered the door, the prince cut off his last head and he fell dead. Inexpressible was the joy of the princess, who told him she was one of the daughters of King Luis and that her two sisters were kept prisoners in the same way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He went outside and kicked the ground, and was brought before another huge rock; after two pails of water and a broken iron bed, he killed the ten-headed monster in the same way, and then the twelve-headed monster of the eldest princess — who, seeing him without his hat, thought he could easily kill him now that he could see him, and 'had scarcely spoken these words when Alberto cut off his remaining head.' Alberto took the princess in his arms, kicked the ground, and all three princesses were carried from palace to palace and brought back to their father's kingdom, for the third day was nearly gone. When they arrived at the palace, King Luis was overjoyed to see his daughters again, and told the prince to decide which one he wanted for a wife. While the three princesses were talking about their life with the monsters, Alberto managed, without being noticed, to give his handkerchief to the youngest. 'Have you decided whom you are going to take for a wife?' said the king the next day. 'The one who has a handkerchief just like mine shall be my wife' — and so the youngest was married to him; for three days banquets of thanksgiving were held, the marriage festivities lasted two days, and the other two princesses were also married to kings' sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 39 'Alberto and the Monsters'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan and Maria: The Beggar's Children Who Became King and Queen
title.zh: 胡安與瑪利亞：乞丐子女封王封后

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (often told by Pampangan grandmothers)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（祖母們常講的故事）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria', eBook #8299

summary.en: Chased from a beggar's hut, Juan and Maria find shelter with a kind old woman; a talking black deer leaves Juan golden armor in its hide, and the hen's egg Maria carries hatches a cock that crows victory at the cockpit. In golden armor Juan wins the tournament for the princess's hand and the throne; a lost prince marries Maria — and both children seek out the parents who drove them off, whose father weeps for his former cruelty.
summary.zh: 被乞丐父母逐出的兄妹胡安與瑪利亞，得善良老嫗收留。黑鹿託夢留金甲於皮中；瑪利亞拾的雞蛋孵出必勝鬥雞。金甲加身的胡安贏得比武、迎娶公主、加冕為王；林中迷途的王子娶瑪利亞為后。兄妹衣錦還鄉探望狠心的父母——父親見子女為王為后，痛哭昔日之殘忍。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Pascual narrator (Arayat); archival record. Fansler compares the Tagalog corrido 'Juan and Maria' and the Tagalog 'Pitong' (Hop o' my Thumb), judging the common source European but the folk-tale nativized.

passages.text: Once there lived in a barrio an old beggar couple who had a son named Juan and a daughter Maria; the proceeds from their begging were hardly enough to support the family. One day, after the old man had returned home from town, he ordered his wife to cook the rice that had been given him; when he saw that the rice was not enough for him and his wife and children, he angrily said to her, 'From now on, don't let me see our children in this house. Chase them as far as you can, and let them find their own food.' The old mother wept when she heard the words of her cruel husband; she did not want to be separated from her children, but she feared that she would be whipped if she kept them, so she obeyed the cruel order. At first the poor children did not want to go away; but, when they saw that their bad father was going to kick them, they ran off crying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon the children came to a wild forest. 'Maria, what will become of us here?' said Juan. 'I am very hungry,' said the little girl. By good luck Juan found a guava-tree with one small fruit on it, climbed up for the guava, and gave it to his hungry sister; and as they were walking along, Maria found a hen's egg on the grass, which she picked up and carried along with her in her dirty ragged skirt. At last they saw a very small hut roofed with dry talahib; an old woman in the hut welcomed them and promised that she would treat them as her little son and daughter. From that time on Juan and Maria lived with the kind old woman: Juan grew to be a strong fine man, spending almost all his time hunting in the mountains and woods, and Maria became a beautiful young woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning Juan caught a black deer; while he was taking the animal home, the deer said to him, 'Juan, as soon as you reach your home, kill me, eat my flesh, and put my hide in your trunk. After three days open your trunk, and you will see something astonishing.' When Juan reached home he did as the deer had told him to do, and on the third day he found in the trunk golden armor — he was greatly delighted by the precious gift. Maria's egg had hatched into a chick which soon grew into a fine fighting cock; one morning the cock crowed, 'Tok-to-ko-kok! Take me to the cockpit. I'll surely win!' — and the next Sunday the rooster was victorious and won much money for Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Juan heard that a tournament would be held in front of the king's palace, the winner of the contest to become the husband of the princess and inherit the throne; Juan quickly put on his golden armor and hastened to the palace to try his skill, defeating all his opponents. The next day his bridal ceremony was celebrated, and the crown was placed on his head; that very day he ascended the throne to rule over the kingdom. Although Juan was now king, he was not proud; he and the queen visited Maria to get her to live in the palace, but the old woman would not allow her to go with her brother, as she had no other companion in the hut. One day a prince was lost in the forest, and happened to come across the hut in which Maria was living; he fell in love with her and wanted to marry her, and as the old woman offered no objections, the following day Maria became a queen, just as her brother had become king. Although the parents of Juan and Maria had been very cruel, yet the king and queen did not forget them: the brother and sister visited their father and mother, whom they found in the most wretched condition, and when the father saw that his children had become king and queen, he wept greatly for his former cruelty to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 40 'Juan and Maria'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pitong: The Seven Brothers and the Giant

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven sons of a poor woodman are twice led to the forest to be abandoned; the wisest, Pitong, marks the way with white stones and then with bread-crumbs the ants devour. Lost, they knock at a banquet-lighted house whose giant husband eats human beings; warned by the wife, Pitong swaps his brothers' rough clothes for the giant's sons' rich garments, so the father's axe at midnight beheads his own children. Escaping with the giant's magic boot, cap, and cane stolen as he sleeps, the boys are carried home, and the powerless giant dies in the woods.
summary.zh: 貧苦樵夫的七個兒子兩度被帶入林中遺棄；最機智的皮通先以白石、後以麵包屑（被螞蟻吃光）記路。迷途中他們投宿巨人妖宅；忠心的女主人示警，皮通讓兄弟們與巨人七子換衣——深夜巨斧落下的，是巨人自己的七個兒子。少年們盜走巨人的魔靴、魔帽、魔杖逃回家中；失去法力的巨人餓斃林中。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Tagalog form of Hop o' my Thumb, which Fansler says must have been received directly from Europe, retaining the received form with few modifications; no other Oriental form recorded.

passages.text: Melanio and Petrona had seven sons; the father was a woodman, and they were so poor that sometimes the whole family went without dinner. One day Melanio said to his wife, 'Petrona, our children are growing, and I don't see how we shall be able to support them all... Don't you think we should get along better without them?' — 'Yes, if we could only get rid of them some way!' — 'Well, to-morrow I will take them to the forest to gather fuel. While they are busy, I will leave them on the pretext of looking for better kinds of wood, and will hurry home. They will not be able to get home, for they won't know the way.' The wife agreed to this cruel plan; but the youngest son overheard the conversation, and told his brothers about it. At last Pitong (seventh), for that was the name of the youngest, and he was the wisest of all, made this suggestion: 'Before we go to the forest to-morrow, I will pick up white stones. I will carry them with me, and as we go along I will drop them one by one... Then, if he leaves us, we can easily follow the track of stones back home.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the children marched straight into the forest with their father as if they were going on a picnic, and Pitong dropped his stones one by one; their father commanded them to get together what sticks they could find, then left them, promising to meet them in a certain place — but really he hurried home and told his wife, 'We are now rid of a heavy burden.' The boys followed the track of stones and reached home safely, and the parents were astounded. The next morning Melanio took his sons out again; this time all the boys took white stones with them, but the part of the forest to which they went was so far that all the stones were used up before they got there — Pitong did not eat his bread, but broke it into pieces and dropped them on the ground as they went along, and the pieces were eaten by the ants. When they could not find the track they cried out, 'Father, father! Where are you?' until they sat down on the ground and began to weep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: It began to grow dark. Pitong advised his brothers to pluck up courage and said to them, 'Follow me.' In about a half-hour they came to a tall tree, and Pitong climbed it: 'Brothers, I see a lighted house from here.' When they came near, they saw that it was well lighted and richly adorned, as if there were a banquet going on — only it was very quiet. Pitong, followed by his brothers, knocked at the door; a woman kindly admitted them, and the boys begged for some food, telling her how they had been deserted by their selfish father. 'I have a giant husband who is a great eater of human beings. If he finds you here, you will surely be devoured; but I can give you something to eat. I will hide you before he comes, and you must remain perfectly still.' The boys had hardly finished dinner when a loud sound was heard from without: 'Here comes my husband! Boys, follow me into that room! You all get into this big trunk and stay here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The door was suddenly flung open: as soon as the giant entered, he said in a fierce voice, 'I smell something human: somebody must be here' — and although the wife did not want to show him the boys, she finally did so, for she feared she would be punished. 'Welcome, my young friends!' said the giant. 'Give these boys some food, and prepare them a comfortable bed. To-morrow early in the morning they will all be killed.' These words increased the terror of the six older brothers, who could not swallow a morsel more of food; but Pitong kept trying to think of a plan by which he could save them all. Now, the room in which they were to sleep was also the room of the giant's seven sons, who were about the same height as the woodman's sons, but had on rich garments. At midnight Pitong awoke his brothers, and they quietly and carefully exchanged clothes with the giant's sons, then pretended to sleep. At four o'clock in the morning the giant came in; he paused before the two beds, but at last turned to the one his sons were in, and when he felt their rough clothes he thought them the strangers, and with his axe he cut off the heads of all seven — his own children. Now Pitong and his six brothers stealthily hurried away into the forest; when the giant found that he had killed his own children he was enraged, and at once took his magic cane, put on his magic boots and cap, and pursued them. The boys hid in a big hole they had dug, and when the keen-scented giant at last leaned against a tree and fell asleep, Pitong called out to his brothers, and they quickly stole the magic boot, cap, and cane of the giant, and were soon carried home. Their parents were very much surprised to see them back, but welcomed their children when they knew of the magic objects; by means of these the family became rich. As for the giant, when he awoke he was deprived of all his power: he was so weak that he could not even get up from the ground, so he died there in the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tagalog folktale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 40, 'Pitong'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Enchanted Prince: The Monkey in the Tallest Tree
title.zh: 被施咒的王子：最高樹上的猿猴

region.zh: 菲律賓卡坦端內斯島維拉克（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince', eBook #8299

summary.en: Forced by his father to marry a woman not the witch he loved, Prince Ucay is cursed: his city becomes a forest of beautiful trees, he a monkey in the tallest tree for five centuries, until a girl loves him more than anything else. Two captured ladies die of fear; a girl disappointed in love, whom a noble look in the monkey's eyes keeps alive, lives on strange fruits until her love outgrows everything — and on the tenth evening she wakes beside a gallant prince, crowned next morning queen of the restored subjects.
summary.zh: 被迫另娶的烏卡伊王子遭女巫詛咒：城池化為秀美之林，他化為最高樹上的猿猴，五百年間唯有真心愛他的少女方能解咒。先前兩位被擄女子皆驚懼而死；唯有一位失戀的姑娘，在猴眼中看出高貴的神情而倖存，以奇果為生，愛意日深——第十夜醒來，身旁已是英俊王子；翌日她加冕為后，全城子民復得人身。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Sorreta narrator (Virac); archival record. Fansler judges it old native tradition, vaguely suggesting the Beauty-and-Beast and Sleeping-Beauty cycles, and notes the number 500 and the monkey-prince suggest Buddhistic lore.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a very rich king in a beautiful city near a wild forest, the home of many wicked witches. The king had a gallant son named Ucay, who fell in love with a beautiful young witch, the daughter of the most bitter enemy of his father. When Ucay became old enough to marry, his father requested him to select the most beautiful lady in the city for his wife; but the prince would neither select one, nor would he tell his father about his love for the witch. So the rich king ordered his soldiers to bring to the palace all the beautiful women that could be found in the kingdom; none of the girls suited the prince, so the king took the matter of selection into his own hands, and, after choosing a very handsome girl, forced his son to marry her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of fear, Ucay consented to do as his father bade him — but the beautiful young witch to whom he had already pledged his love became angry with him for his timidity, and so she resolved to change the city into a forest of beautiful trees. Her fickle lover she transformed into a monkey, who should live in the tallest tree, and who should not be able to recover his human shape till five centuries had passed, when a charming girl would live with him and love him more than anything else; moreover, she changed the king's subjects into other animals as she pleased. No sooner had the marriage of the prince been proclaimed, then, than the desire of the witch was accomplished, to the great surprise of the neighboring cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Four centuries had already passed; the wonderful disappearance of the city was already forgotten, and people from other places began to build houses in the enchanted city. The monkey-prince was always watching for an opportunity to catch a beautiful girl who should break the spell that kept him in his miserable condition; soon a church was built near the foot of the tree in which he lived. He had already succeeded in capturing two ladies, but they had died of fear. After incalculable suffering and extraordinary patience, the time for his recovery came at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One Sunday morning before the mass was over, a very beautiful girl, the daughter of a poor man, came out of the church and sat at the foot of the tree; she had been disappointed in her love with a rich man's son, who had forsaken her in order to marry the daughter of a rich man, so she wished to die. When the monkey-prince saw her sitting there alone, he noiselessly went down, carefully took her by the right hand, and carried her to the top of the tree. She would have died of fright, as was the fate of the two former women, had she not seen in the monkey's eyes a noble look that filled her with wonder and sympathy. As days went by, she lived on delicious fruits which were entirely strange to her; and her love for the poor creature grew greater and greater, until at last she loved him more than anything else. On the evening of the tenth day she was surprised to find herself beside a gallant prince in a richly-decorated room; at first she thought she was dreaming, but when the prince woke up, kissed her, and then told her the history of his life, she knew that it was real — 'Ah, me! God is wise!' The next morning she was crowned queen of her husband's happy subjects, whom she had restored from the enchantment of the wicked witch; every one in the kingdom loved his new queen as long as he lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 41 'The Enchanted Prince'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince's Dream: The Mirror of the King of the Demons

region.en: Tigaon, Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區蒂高安（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dream-ghost sends the prince to the city of Black, then home to his own cellar, where he finds diamond columns and a final chamber that 'none can unlock but the wealthiest Negro in the city of Black.' The Negro leads him through the sphinx-ferry and fire-gated walls to the king of the demons, who demands in exchange a woman 'whose heart is untainted by any worldly passion' — tested by an oval mirror that clouds at a false heart. The one pure girl is a poor farmer's daughter, whom the prince falls in love with on the road; the demon, unveiling the veiled figures in the final chamber, gives her to the prince — but keeps the diamond column.
summary.zh: 夢中幽靈引王子至『黑城』又折返自家地窖，尋得鑽石柱與最後密室——『唯黑城首富能開』。黑人引他渡獅身人面之舟、過雷火之門，謁見魔王；魔王索求一位『心無塵欲』的女子為酬——以一面照心的橢圓魔鏡驗之。純真的女子竟是貧農之女；王子途中愛上她。魔王揭開帷中人——竟將姑娘賜予王子，卻收回了鑽石柱。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Tigaon, Camarines); archival record. Fansler notes (per Boas) that the story is from the Arabian Nights 'The Tale of Zayn Al-Asnam.'

passages.text: Once there lived a young prince who, after his father's death, succeeded to the throne as the sole heir of a vast, rich kingdom. He indulged himself in all worldly pleasures, gave dances, and all sorts of merry-making surrounded his court; meanwhile the royal treasury was being drained, and his subjects were becoming disloyal to him. Disappointed by his conduct, his counsellors plotted to dismiss him from the realm; the prince's mother, the widowed queen, learned of their plot and said to him, 'My son, I wish you would turn from your foolish trifling, and govern your people as you ought to do; for your advisers are planning to dethrone you.' The prince, who was not bad at heart, followed his mother's sensible advice, and his ministers gave up their plan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One noon, when the prince was taking his siesta, he had a dream: a ghost appeared to him and spoke in this manner, 'Your father left a hidden treasure of gold and diamonds, which he forgot to mention in his will. Should you care to have that treasure, go to the city of Black. There you will find a Negro, the richest in that city, who will tell you all about the treasure.' 'Undeceive yourself,' said his mother. 'Never believe in dreams.' In spite of her words he set out disguised as a poor traveller; the gates were closed for the night, and while he slept outside the walls the very same ghost appeared to him: 'Go back to your palace, prince, and there in the cellar you will find the treasure I spoke of.' Early one morning, without the knowledge of his mother, he took a pointed iron bar and went down into the cellar, digging until his bar struck something hard which produced a metallic sound; he uncovered an iron platform locked with a padlock, and beneath it a low ladder made of diamond bars, leading down into a small apartment all shining bright as if it were day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He found two columns of diamond bars, each a foot in thickness and a metre in height, whose brightness shot through all the corners like sunbeams; the subterranean chamber led to another with a big safe, from which gold coins flowed like water in torrents from a cliff. 'Are these gold coins and diamonds real, or am I simply dreaming?' — he filled his cap with the coins and went up into the sunlight to assure himself they were of pure gold. In a third chamber were two more columns of diamonds; in a fourth, behind a wide curtain of silk on which were embroidered in big golden letters the words: 'Inside this chamber is another column of diamonds twice as large and twice as high as those in the other two; none can unlock this apartment but the wealthiest Negro in the city of Black.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Disguised again as a poor traveller, the prince found the Negro, who received him kindly — and, hearing the prince's story, knelt down before him: 'My prince, I was the most beloved servant of your father. I acknowledge you as my master... There is but one man who can unlock it, who knows very well your dead father, and who was his friend... This man is the king of the demons. And to him we will go together.' They feasted, then journeyed to the palace of the king of the demons, crossing a river in a banca paddled by a sphinx and passing through two circular walls — at the knock of the first gate it became dark all around them, lightnings flashed, and it thundered; at the second gate two lions ran out with eyes glowing like balls of fire, ready to devour them — until, recognizing the Negro, these two kings of beasts wagged their tails as a sign of welcome. 'I gave that diamond column to your father as a gift which he might bequeath to his son; and if you are his son, you shall have it. But, before giving it to you, I should like to have you do me a favor in return for that rich gift. If you will bring me a very beautiful woman to be my companion, one whose heart is untainted by any worldly passion, I will unlock for you your wished-for treasure, the diamond room.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king of the demons gave the prince a small oval mirror: 'If you see a beautiful woman, hold this mirror before her face. If the surface of the mirror becomes clouded, leave her; but if the surface of the mirror remains as clear as before, bring her to me, for she is the one I want for my comfort.' In three days they searched through three cities and three villages, but every girl that looked on the magic mirror clouded its surface — until, resting in a small village on their discouraged return, they found a most beautiful girl, the daughter of a poor farmer, whose looking on the mirror left its surface as clear as before. On the way the prince, fascinated by her beauty, fell in love with the girl, and did not want to give her up to the king of the demons; but the Negro would not consent, and the prince gave up his plan on condition that the girl's face be veiled. When they arrived at the palace, the king of the demons gladly met them: 'Now you have fulfilled my wish. You may go back to your palace, and there you will find the diamond apartment unlocked for you.' The sorrowing prince went home with heavy heart, no longer thinking of the treasure but of the beautiful maiden he had given up. Yet, to divert his mind, he went to the subterranean apartment, where he found the last chamber unlocked; inside were two veiled figures, the one in the form of a king with his sceptre and crown, the other a maiden. He unveiled the one with the crown and was astounded to find the very same king of the demons. 'Prince, unveil that figure,' said the king of the demons — and the young king did so, and to his great joy saw the beautiful maiden he had lost his heart to. 'Young king, since on your way to my palace you fell in love with this maiden, I deem it fit that you should have her for your companion; but do not expect the diamond column any more.' Then the king of the demons disappeared; the prince at once embraced the maiden and conducted her up to his palace, and that same day their marriage was celebrated with pomp and luxury.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 42 'The Prince's Dream'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wicked Woman's Reward: The Corpse the Birds Would Not Give Up

region.en: Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (told by a father to his son)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區甘馬粦（父親講給兒子聽的故事）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward', eBook #8299

summary.en: A jealous concubine smothers her own daughter, steals her rival's boy and puts a newborn cat in its place; the king drowns the accused mother without investigation and marries the thief. But the drowned woman's corpse floats fragrant down the river, covered by the birds with flowers — and when the king comes to see the miracle, the corpse rises and tells him of the theft before sinking away. He hurls the treacherous wife from the palace window, buries the innocent woman among the noble dead, and her son grows to rule the kingdom well.
summary.zh: 妒忌的侍妾悶死親女、竊走情敵之子，以新生的小貓掉包。國王未經查問便將被誣者沉河，並娶竊賊為妻。然而被溺女屍順流而飄，芳香撲鼻，群鳥啣花覆體——國王親臨觀奇，屍身忽起，泣訴冤情而後沉去。暴怒的國王將惡婦拋出窗外、懸屔示眾，以王禮厚葬無辜者；其子長成，治國有道。

sensitivity.note: Bicol tale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Camarines); archival record. Animal-substitution motif; Fansler knows no other versions of the story as a whole.

passages.text: Once there lived a certain king. He had concubines, five in number; two of them he loved more than the others, for they were to bear him children, and he said that the one who should give birth to a male baby he would marry. Soon one of them bore a child, but it was a girl, and shortly afterward the other bore a handsome boy. The one which had given birth to the baby girl was restless: she wished that she might have the boy, and in order to satisfy her wish thought of an ingenious plan whereby she might get possession of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One midnight, when all were sound asleep, she killed her own baby and secretly buried it; then she quietly crept to her rival's bed and stole her boy, putting in his place a newborn cat. Early in the morning the king went to the room of his concubine who had borne the boy, and was surprised to find a cat by her side instead of a human child; he was so enraged that he immediately ordered her to be drowned in the river, and his order was at once executed. Then he went into the room of the wicked woman: the moment he saw the boy baby he was filled with great joy, and he smothered the child with kisses; as he had promised, he married the woman, sent away all his other concubines, and harbored a deep love for his deceitful wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon afterwards there was a great confusion throughout the kingdom: everybody wondered why it was that the river smelled so fragrant, and the people were very anxious to find out the cause of the sweet odor. It was not many days before the townspeople along the river-bank found the corpse of the drowned woman floating in the water — and this was the source of the sweetness that was causing their restlessness; it was full of many different kinds of flowers which had been gathered by the birds. When the people attempted to remove the corpse from the water, the birds pecked them, and would not let the body be taken away. At last the news of the miracle was brought to the ears of the king, who himself went to the river to see the wonderful corpse; as soon as he saw the figure of the drowned woman, he was tortured with remorse — then, to his great surprise and fear, the corpse suddenly stood up out of the water, and said to him in sorrowful tones, 'O king! As you see, my body has been floating on the water. The birds would have buried me, but I wanted you to know that you ordered me to be killed without any investigation of my fault. Your wife stole my boy, and, as you saw, she put a cat by my side.' The ghost vanished, and the king saw the body float away again down the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king at once ordered the body of his favorite to be taken out of the water and brought to the palace, and he himself was driven back to the town, violent with rage and remorse; there he seized his treacherous wife and hurled her out of the window of the palace, and he even ordered her body to be hanged. Having gotten rid of this evil woman, the king ordered the body of the innocent woman to be buried among the noble dead: the corpse was placed in a magnificent tomb, and was borne in a procession with pompous funeral ceremonies; he himself dressed entirely in black as a sign of his genuine grief for her. Yet, in spite of his sorrow for his true wife, he took comfort in her son, who grew to be a handsome boy; as time went on the prince developed into a brave youth, able to perform the duties of his father the king — so, as his father became old, no longer able to bear the responsibilities of regal power, the prince succeeded to the throne and ruled the kingdom well, proving himself to be the son of the good woman by his wise and just rule over his subjects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 43 'The Wicked Woman's Reward'; not verbatim.
